article-004.text: Which statement best summarises how the CDC describes ADHD?
options: It is a short-term behavioural phase that most children quickly outgrow.
It is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control into adulthood.
It is caused primarily by parents setting inconsistent rules.
It is diagnosed whenever a child is occasionally restless.
article-004.evidence: ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders of childhood. It is usually first diagnosed in childhood and often lasts into adulthood.

article-004.text: How does predominantly inattentive ADHD differ from predominantly hyperactive-impulsive ADHD?
options: It mainly involves difficulty organising, focusing and following instructions, rather than restlessness and impulsivity.
It affects adults only, while hyperactive-impulsive ADHD affects children only.
It is always less severe and never affects schoolwork.
It is identified by increased physical activity rather than attention difficulties.
article-004.evidence: Predominantly Inattentive Presentation: It is hard for the individual to organize or finish a task, to pay attention to details, or to follow instructions or conversations.

article-004.text: What can reasonably be concluded from the discussion of ADHD causes?
options: Research has established excessive sugar intake as the leading cause.
ADHD is unrelated to genetic factors.
Environmental conditions have all been ruled out.
Genetics appears important, but the full range of causes and risk factors is not yet known.
article-004.evidence: The cause(s) and risk factors for ADHD are unknown, but current research shows that genetics plays an important role.

article-004.text: Why does the CDC recommend several steps when diagnosing ADHD?
options: Because symptoms must be present in every family member.
Because only a blood test can establish the condition.
Because other conditions can produce similar symptoms and there is no single definitive ADHD test.
Because parents' observations have no diagnostic value.
article-004.evidence: There is no single test to diagnose ADHD, and many other problems, like anxiety, depression, sleep problems, and certain types of learning disabilities, can have similar symptoms.

article-004.text: What approach is recommended first for preschool-aged children with ADHD?
options: Permanent removal from ordinary school settings.
Behaviour therapy, especially parent training, before trying medication.
Waiting until adulthood before seeking any support.
Medication without any follow-up or adjustment.
article-004.evidence: For preschool-aged children (4-5 years of age) with ADHD, behavior therapy, particularly training for parents, is recommended as the first line of treatment before medication is tried.

article-005.text: What central question does the writer explore by comparing Usain Bolt with the fictional Flash?
options: Whether fictional superheroes can train professional athletes.
Whether any sprinter has ever competed against a cheetah.
Whether there are biological limits to how fast humans can run.
Whether advanced running shoes can reverse ageing.
article-005.evidence: Is there a biological limit to how fast humans can run? Or will we all be sprinting like The Flash in future?

article-005.text: Why does Mark Denny consider it possible that Bolt's 100-metre record is close to the ultimate human limit?
options: His analysis of many racing records suggests performances tend to level off over time.
Every sport has already prohibited further training improvements.
Human muscles can contract without physical constraints.
Bolt's record was set before reliable timing technology existed.
article-005.evidence: Performances were clearly plateauing in all races

article-005.text: What distinction does the article make between four-legged sprinters and human runners?
options: Both are anatomically designed exclusively for long-distance endurance.
Humans are better suited to short bursts because their spines are more flexible.
Four-legged animals cannot reach high speeds without genetic engineering.
Animals such as cheetahs are built for short-term speed, whereas two-legged humans are better suited to endurance.
article-005.evidence: Four-legged animals like cheetahs – with their long legs, light body weight and flexible spine – are designed for short-term speed. Bipedal runners, meanwhile, are built for endurance.

article-005.text: Why would simply making a runner taller or giving them heavier bones not necessarily improve their maximum speed?
options: Height has no relationship of any kind to stride length.
Changes that could increase speed introduce limits or extra weight elsewhere in the body.
Increased height always eliminates muscle strength.
Longer legs prevent all movement at high speed.
article-005.evidence: Even if you made the bones more robust, they would then be heavier, negating what you’re trying to do.

article-005.text: What possibility does Denny suggest might allow future humans to move beyond their current biological speed limits?
options: Reaching the speed of light through ordinary sprint training.
Repeating the exact same training methods indefinitely.
Genetic engineering that changes muscle and body structures.
Replacing all competitive running with horse racing.
article-005.evidence: The only way you could go beyond these biological limits, says Denny, is with genetic engineering.

article-008.text: What is the interviewee's overall view of AI-generated art?
options: AI tools can assist artists, but genuine creativity and judgement remain primarily human.
AI has already developed human-like emotions and independent artistic opinions.
AI should replace artists because it never makes mistakes.
AI creativity no longer depends on the work of humans.
article-008.evidence: It’s a creative process that’s mainly human and AI is following the rules.

article-008.text: How do text-to-image AI models learn to connect a prompt with visual objects?
options: They rely entirely on a human to draw every requested image in real time.
They infer the meaning of words from captions paired with large numbers of training images.
They are programmed with a complete dictionary of every possible scene.
They automatically verify all images against objective truth before training.
article-008.evidence: This worked by training the model on lots of images and their accompanying text caption to understand how the words relate to the images.

article-008.text: Why are generative image models especially prone to mistakes in small details such as hands?
options: Human viewers are generally unable to notice such mistakes.
The systems deliberately refuse to generate human anatomy.
Small details are absent from all their training pictures.
Their optimisation prioritises getting the overall image right rather than every small feature.
article-008.evidence: The AI neglects the small details that we, as humans, are tuned to catch – a hand with four fingers or a three-legged person, for example.

article-008.text: What makes training large image-generation systems environmentally costly?
options: Most images have to be physically printed before they can be used.
The models can run only on devices powered by fossil fuels.
They require extensive processing on energy-consuming GPUs over long periods.
The interview claims digital images use no electricity during training.
article-008.evidence: The training process for these models requires a lot of energy. You need to run them on graphical processing units (GPUs) for weeks while they process billions of images.

article-008.text: What is the interviewee's main concern about the way current image models are trained?
options: They use large numbers of artists' internet images without obtaining the artists' consent.
They learn exclusively from photographs owned by the person using the tool.
They have completely solved questions of artistic ownership.
All training images are made by the model without any human source material.
article-008.evidence: The copyright issue comes with the use of millions of images taken from the internet without consent of the artist.

article-040.text: What central problem does Christopher Reddy believe scientists must address?
options: They should withdraw completely from public debate.
Researchers should explain their work more clearly to non-specialists during crises.
Scientific research should stop whenever the public disagrees.
The media should replace scientists in explaining technical evidence.
article-040.evidence: The core problem is rooted in academia itself: communication with non-scientists is not appreciated

article-040.text: What did Reddy learn from his early research on oil spills?
options: The research had no practical use in disasters.
Government agencies always apply new evidence immediately.
The public can understand only research published in academic journals.
Useful scientific findings may be ignored when researchers do not communicate with those who need them.
article-040.evidence: industry and cleanup specialists rarely paid attention to the developing science, in part because researchers like him were not talking to those who might make use of their work.

article-040.text: How do the expectations of the public and scientists differ during a crisis, according to Reddy?
options: Scientists may accept prolonged uncertainty, while members of the public often want immediate clear answers.
Both groups expect every complex research problem to be solved within seconds.
The public generally welcomes years of uncertainty more than researchers do.
Scientists prefer instant certainty and avoid examining evidence.
article-040.evidence: A scientist is more than willing to wait weeks, months, years, even decades to solve an outstanding research question. The public wants certainty, and they want it in four seconds.

article-040.text: Why might scientists hesitate to offer a clear explanation in public?
options: They are legally forbidden to speak about their studies.
They believe scientific accuracy requires never speaking to journalists.
They fear professional criticism or lasting damage to their reputations if they make a mistake.
They think journalists always understand uncertainty better than specialists.
article-040.evidence: When you venture outside of the ivory tower and make a mistake, more often than not the risk is greater than the reward

article-040.text: Why does the article discuss the Deepwater Horizon oil spill?
options: To argue that environmental research should end after a disaster.
To illustrate how scientific expertise can be crucial yet poorly understood or communicated during an emergency.
To prove that oil spills pose no environmental risks.
To show that every disagreement between the media and researchers was resolved instantly.
article-040.evidence: Initial containment, damage assessment and environmental restoration work all hinged on our contributions.

article-006.text: Why are the carvings at La Roche-Cotard cave significant to archaeologists?
options: They prove that modern humans invented all European cave art.
They may be among the earliest surviving examples of art made by Neanderthals.
They show that early Europeans used written alphabets.
They reveal that Neanderthals lived exclusively in caves.
article-006.evidence: The engravings are some of the oldest known examples of Neanderthal art and are possibly the very oldest.

article-006.text: What combination of evidence supports the attribution of the cave markings to Neanderthals?
options: Modern human skeletons and Roman coins found in the chamber.
Written records left by the cave's occupants.
The absence of any stone tools and evidence of modern habitation.
Mousterian tools associated with Neanderthals and the ancient sealing of the cave entrance.
article-006.evidence: The attribution of the engravings to Neanderthals, not modern humans, rests partly on the distinctive Mousterian tools found in the cave and partly on the timing.

article-006.text: What does the article indicate about the meaning of the engravings?
options: Researchers cannot yet confidently establish whether they had a shared symbolic meaning.
Each marking has been translated as a specific word.
They were definitely maps of Neanderthal hunting grounds.
Their purpose is known from accompanying written inscriptions.
article-006.evidence: It isn’t clear whether the engravings “represent symbolic thinking”

article-006.text: How does April Nowell distinguish this evidence from the art associated with Homo sapiens?
options: Neanderthal engravings always contain longer repeated sequences.
There is no evidence that modern humans produced symbolic objects.
The Neanderthal examples appear relatively isolated, unlike more frequent recurring elements in H. sapiens art.
Both traditions are known only from a single cave.
article-006.evidence: There are no other known Neanderthal sites with engravings like those in La Roche-Cotard or Gorham’s cave – whereas prehistoric art by H. sapiens is more common and contains repeating elements.

article-006.text: What possibility does Paola Villa raise about symbolic behaviour?
options: Neanderthals learned all symbolism from medieval people.
Modern humans may have learned or developed some symbolic behaviours through contact with Neanderthals.
Both populations remained completely isolated from one another.
Symbolic behaviour disappeared as soon as modern humans arrived.
article-006.evidence: It may be that modern humans picked up some symbolic Neanderthal behaviours and developed them, says Villa.

article-007.text: What does the author argue about people's ability to recognise liars?
options: Ordinary people are consistently accurate when reading facial expressions.
Body language provides a scientifically reliable lie detector.
Even deliberate deception can be difficult to identify, despite popular beliefs about telltale behaviour.
The ability to spot lies depends solely on the listener's education.
article-007.evidence: The weight of empirical research shows it’s hard to identify even very purposeful liars from their behaviour.

article-007.text: What does the 2006 meta-analysis of deception judgments suggest?
options: People's ability to distinguish lies from truths is only slightly better than chance.
Most people identify deception correctly in virtually every case.
People become accurate lie detectors after hearing one convincing story.
The analysis found that liars share one unmistakable physical gesture.
article-007.evidence: looked at more than 200 studies to find that people’s accuracy when distinguishing truth from lies isn’t much better than chance.

article-007.text: Why might a charming friend be especially convincing when telling an implausible story?
options: Close friends usually provide independent proof for all their claims.
Attractive people cannot deliberately lie to people they know.
A friend's physical appearance always reveals whether they are dishonest.
Trust and intimacy may lower the listener's guard and make the friend's account easier to accept.
article-007.evidence: The flipside of heightened intimacy is lowered guards.

article-007.text: What is the purpose of the author's account of the woman called Julia?
options: To show that lies occur only between strangers.
To illustrate how an apparently caring person's false claims can undermine others' trust in their perceptions.
To prove that Julia's claims were confirmed by independent investigators.
To suggest that everybody knowingly accepts dishonesty in their relationships.
article-007.evidence: Over time my trust in my judgment eroded.

article-007.text: Which conclusion best follows from the article's discussion of deceptive behaviour?
options: The listener's assumptions and relationship with the speaker can influence whether a lie is believed.
A person's posture alone is sufficient to establish the truth.
A liar who believes their story will always confess immediately.
Empirical research proves that every deceptive person looks away while speaking.
article-007.evidence: People who convince themselves of their own truthfulness while being dishonest may act no differently to normal.

article-009.text: What is the article's overall position on the fall of the Roman Empire?
options: Rome ended on a single date for one universally accepted reason.
Its decline was a complex process involving multiple causes, and even the idea of a straightforward 'fall' is debated.
The empire ended only because it expanded into North Africa.
All scholars agree that the empire survived unchanged.
article-009.evidence: Just as the Fall of Rome was not caused by a single event, the way Rome fell was also complex.

article-009.text: Why is identifying one precise date for Rome's fall problematic?
options: No Roman historical records have survived.
The Roman Empire existed for less than a decade.
The city of Rome never served as an imperial centre.
Changes occurred over a long period and the empire's political and geographic structure altered.
article-009.evidence: In fact, during the period of imperial decline, the empire actually expanded.

article-009.text: What political change did the division between East and West bring?
options: Every province immediately became an independent state.
Rome permanently became the capital of both halves.
New imperial centres developed, including Constantinople in the East and Milan in the West.
The Roman army was abolished throughout the empire.
article-009.evidence: The schism of east and west created not just an eastern capital first in Nicomedia and then Constantinople, but also a move in the west from Rome to Milan.

article-009.text: What role does Christianity play in one interpretation of Rome's decline?
options: Growing church influence and new religious allegiances could conflict with existing imperial authority and traditions.
Christianity was the established state religion throughout the empire's entire history.
Church leaders always supported the deification of emperors.
Religion is ruled out as a relevant factor by every historian quoted.
article-009.evidence: Over time, Christian church leaders became increasingly influential, eroding the emperors' powers.

article-009.text: How does the account complicate the portrayal of outsiders as merely enemies of Rome?
options: Outsiders never entered imperial territory.
They contributed soldiers and revenue to Rome even as the empire later lost territory and resources to some of them.
They supplied Rome with no military personnel or taxes.
All groups described as barbarians acted in exactly the same way.
article-009.evidence: The barbarians, which is a term that covers a varied and changing group of outsiders, were embraced by Rome, who used them as suppliers of tax revenue and bodies for the military

article-010.text: How does the article describe the development of mental strength?
options: As a fixed trait that cannot change after childhood.
As an automatic result of professional success.
As something that depends mainly on avoiding difficulties.
As a capacity strengthened through deliberate practice and everyday habits.
article-010.evidence: cultivating mental strength isn’t automatic. Instead, it demands regular exercise and mindful practice

article-010.text: Why does the writer recommend regular self-reflection?
options: To avoid having to make decisions independently.
To better recognise emotions, motivations and responses, and learn from past experiences.
To remove the need to interact with other people.
To ensure that every decision is free from uncertainty.
article-010.evidence: This practice offers opportunities to analyze past actions, learn from successes and failures, and gain insights into how they might improve.

article-010.text: What attitude towards change characterises mentally strong individuals in the article?
options: They resist every unfamiliar situation regardless of the consequences.
They expect their plans never to require adjustment.
They treat new circumstances as potential opportunities and adapt their plans when necessary.
They see adaptability as a sign that their goals do not matter.
article-010.evidence: They view change not as a threat but as an opportunity for growth.

article-010.text: What does the author's discussion of persistence imply about failure?
options: Setbacks can provide lessons rather than marking the end of progress.
Strong people avoid all situations in which they might fail.
Achieving a goal requires never changing an ineffective approach.
People should immediately abandon goals when they meet resistance.
article-010.evidence: They understand that setbacks and failures form part of the journey and serve as vital learning opportunities.

article-010.text: How does the writer distinguish optimism from ignoring problems?
options: Optimism requires pretending that challenges do not exist.
Optimism removes the need for rest or self-care.
A positive attitude can be maintained only when life is easy.
Optimism involves recognising difficulties while focusing on constructive possibilities.
article-010.evidence: Positivity is not about ignoring the difficulties of life. Instead, it involves acknowledging challenges and focusing on the bright side of situations.

article-011.text: What is the article's central argument about why food tastes delicious?
options: It depends entirely on the number of taste buds a person has.
It results exclusively from the food's chemical composition.
Flavour emerges from sensory signals together with experience, expectations and context.
It is determined before birth and cannot be influenced by learning.
article-011.evidence: our biases filter the taste experience

article-011.text: What does the discovery of taste receptors outside the mouth suggest?
options: Taste-related biology is more complex and widespread than the traditional tongue-only account.
The mouth plays no role in how food is experienced.
Taste receptors work only when people are asleep.
The discovery proves that personal preferences are identical for everyone.
article-011.evidence: scientists have found taste receptors all over the body

article-011.text: Why does the writer distinguish the physiology of flavour from what people like to eat?
options: Because the body's digestive system operates independently of the brain.
Because understanding sensory mechanisms alone does not explain individual food preferences.
Because food preferences cannot change at any age.
Because taste can be explained only through genetics.
article-011.evidence: This physiology may explain what we mean by flavor—but anatomy doesn't much help us understand what we like.

article-011.text: What does the example involving researchers, food pictures and mild electrical stimulation illustrate?
options: Food preference depends exclusively on the temperature of the tongue.
Electricity can permanently replace every taste receptor.
People can accurately identify flavours without any sensory input.
Expectations and other sensory cues can influence how taste is experienced.
article-011.evidence: researchers connected volunteers' tongues to a low-voltage electrical device, showed them pictures of food items

article-011.text: Which conclusion best reflects the writer's discussion of deliciousness?
options: A meal's social and personal setting may shape its perceived flavour.
A food's appeal is fixed by its nutritional content alone.
People's childhood experiences have no connection with taste.
Taste preferences are fully explained by anatomy.
article-011.evidence: Deliciousness comes from our mother, our childhood, the room we are eating in, the plates we are eating on and the friends

article-012.text: Which claim does the neuroscience columnist principally seek to challenge?
options: That sleep influences memory formation.
That humans normally use only 10 per cent of their brains.
That the brain requires energy to function.
That scientific findings can be misunderstood.
article-012.evidence: THE IDEA THAT WE ONLY USE 10 PER CENT OF OUR BRAINS IS A MYTH THAT NEEDS TO DIE

article-012.text: Why does the author compare an underused brain to a supercomputer used only as a clock?
options: To argue that brains literally operate like car computers.
To suggest that the brain has no specialised functions.
To illustrate how implausibly wasteful it would be to maintain such an expensive organ while using almost none of it.
To claim technology can replace the human brain.
article-012.evidence: having a brain as biologically demanding as ours but only using 10 per cent of it, is like bolting a giant supercomputer onto your sports car just to set the clock

article-012.text: According to the writer, why can the 10-per-cent myth be harmful?
options: It provides an apparent justification for unfounded claims about untapped brain powers.
It causes the brain to stop processing visual information.
It has conclusively disproved modern neuroscience.
It makes all brain training scientifically impossible.
article-012.evidence: the ‘we only use 10 per cent of our brain’ myth provides a huge ‘unknown’ space in which pseudoscientific/bogus brain-based claims can hide

article-012.text: What does the discussion of the myth's possible origins suggest?
options: Its exact inventor has been identified beyond dispute.
It was invented only after magnetic brain scanning became widespread.
It has been disproved only in the past few months.
Its precise origins are uncertain, but the idea has circulated for well over a century.
article-012.evidence: even though the true origins of the myth remain unclear, one thing we can say for certain is that they go back a long way

article-012.text: What broader lesson does the writer draw from the persistence of the myth?
options: Modern research should never revise earlier ideas.
Old or incomplete findings should not be turned into sweeping claims about how the brain works.
Scientific understanding remains unchanged for centuries.
Misconceptions disappear automatically when evidence improves.
article-012.evidence: the dangers of forming blanket conclusions based on very old research

article-013.text: What is the main theme of the readers' responses to the question about a person who has never suffered?
options: The importance of eliminating every ordinary frustration.
The certainty that hardship always improves character.
The difficulty of predicting personality without adversity, because people learn and respond differently.
The claim that empathy is a purely inherited trait.
article-013.evidence: The few who have experienced none of this could be functional, successful, happy, but could also be oblivious, entitled and judgmental.

article-013.text: What does the example of the child upset by a stolen ice cream suggest?
options: Experiences that seem minor to others may still feel intensely distressing to an individual.
Only adults can recognise emotional distress.
Any disappointment is necessarily traumatic.
Children who have stable lives are never disappointed.
article-013.evidence: when a seagull stole her ice- cream, she screamed and burst into tears

article-013.text: Why do some contributors warn against assuming that a hardship-free person would be automatically kind?
options: They believe empathy can arise only from severe injury.
They argue that happiness is incompatible with moral behaviour.
They assume everyone who is wealthy lacks sympathy.
Without perspective on others' difficulties, someone might become entitled or judgmental.
article-013.evidence: if they decided that bad things must only happen to bad people, or they’re somehow above everyone else’s problems

article-013.text: What conclusion follows from the claim that two people can experience the same event differently?
options: Trauma depends only on the event's public seriousness.
Individual reactions to difficult experiences differ rather than following one universal pattern.
Every adverse experience produces identical long-term effects.
No one can be harmed by experiences shared with others.
article-013.evidence: two people could have the exact same experience and one of them be traumatised and the other not

article-013.text: How does the discussion of stories and fiction complicate the original thought experiment?
options: It suggests that people can acquire emotional understanding indirectly through others' experiences.
It proves that fiction prevents people from feeling pain.
It treats personal experience as the only source of empathy.
It argues that books can replace all social relationships.

article-014.text: What is the article primarily reporting about The Simpsons and the missing submersible?
options: The show directly assisted the Coast Guard's investigation.
The show's writers had received confidential information about the voyage.
Fans noticed apparent similarities between an older fictional episode and a real maritime emergency.
The cartoon caused the submersible's navigation system to fail.
article-014.evidence: ‘The Simpsons’ fans say show predicted Titanic submarine disappearance 17 years ago

article-014.text: Why did viewers connect a previous Simpsons story with the Titan incident?
options: The episode had already documented the real passenger list.
A fictional underwater exploration scene resembled elements of the later search for the missing vessel.
The programme had been filmed on board the real vessel.
The animation contained an official Coast Guard report.
article-014.evidence: After exploring for a bit, the duo comes across the remains of a massive ship filled to the brim with treasure.

article-014.text: According to the report, what made the search for the submersible urgent?
options: The vessel had been missing for years.
Its passengers were known to be safely ashore.
The submersible was carrying hazardous radioactive material.
Five people were aboard and contact was lost during a deep-water dive.
article-014.evidence: lost contact with the crew about an hour and 45 minutes into the dive

article-014.text: How should the social media comments about the writers' supposed prediction be understood?
options: As reactions from fans rather than proof that the writers knew future events.
As verified evidence of advance knowledge held by the show's producers.
As official statements by maritime safety investigators.
As scientific findings about predicting accidents.
article-014.evidence: The Simpson writers should be investigated because this is insane

article-014.text: What additional concern about submersible safety appears in the report?
options: The vessel was required to use only renewable fuel.
Criticism had been raised about inadequate non-destructive testing of the hull.
The crew had been ordered not to communicate with surface vessels.
Every component had passed all possible independent safety checks.
article-014.evidence: lack of non-destructive testing performed on the hull of the Titan

article-015.text: What conclusion did the Coast Guard draw from the debris found in the North Atlantic?
options: The missing vessel had safely reached the Titanic wreck.
The reported underwater noises were definitely produced by the passengers.
The evidence indicated that the submersible had suffered a catastrophic implosion.
The submersible was still transmitting from beneath the surface.
article-015.evidence: a debris field located in the North Atlantic suggests that a submersible missing since Sunday, with five passengers on board, suffered a "catastrophic implosion"

article-015.text: Why were the underwater noises reported during the search initially significant?
options: They offered a possible lead, although investigators could not establish that they came from the missing vessel.
They confirmed that the passengers had safely left the submersible.
They were identified as messages sent by the vessel's onboard radio.
They immediately revealed the precise location of the wreck.
article-015.evidence: hopes were raised when a Canadian plane picked up underwater noises, but the US Coast Guard was unable to confirm they were from the sub

article-015.text: What happened when remotely operated vehicles were moved to investigate the reported sounds?
options: They recovered all passengers alive.
They successfully located the source of each noise.
They were withdrawn before reaching the search zone.
Their search did not produce a positive result.
article-015.evidence: ROV operations had been relocated "in an attempt to explore the origin of the noises", but "yielded negative results"

article-015.text: What does the article's account of the loss of contact suggest about the search operation?
options: The vessel was tracked continuously during the entire descent.
The incident became apparent only after communications stopped during the descent and the vessel failed to return as expected.
Authorities had confirmed the incident before the dive began.
No search coordination was needed because the vessel resurfaced on time.
article-015.evidence: Contact was lost one hour and 45 minutes into its descent

article-015.text: Which statement best describes the eventual search response?
options: The search expanded indefinitely with all rescue craft remaining deployed.
Investigators concluded that debris provided no useful information.
The main search began winding down while remotely operated vehicles remained at the site.
The Coast Guard immediately abandoned all underwater examination.
article-015.evidence: The search is being wound down over the next 24 hours, although remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) will remain on site.
